title: Searching level by level
objectives: Implement breadth-first search with a queue.
Mark nodes seen as they join the queue, and use `deque` for the queue

screens.title: A rumour spreads
screens.prose: A rumour starts at A on day 0. Each day, everyone who knows it tells all their neighbours.
screens.question: Tap every node that first hears the rumour on day 2.

hints.text: Who hears on day 1? Then who do they tell?
B and D hear on day 1.
B tells E. D tells C and F. A already knows.

feedback.correct: C, E and F hear on day 2.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find day 1 first, then the new nodes next to day 1.

byKey.cumulative: You tapped everyone who knows by day 2. Tap only the nodes hearing it for the first time.
byKey.G: G hears on day 3: every route from A to G has three edges.
byKey.H: H hears on day 3, through B and then E.
byKey.B: B is next to A, so B hears on day 1.

explain.text: Day 1 is A's neighbours, B and D. Day 2 is the new nodes next to them: E, C and F. Spreading one ring at a time is **breadth-first search**, or BFS.

canvas.caption: Day 0: A. Day 1: B, D. Day 2: E, C, F. Day 3: G, H.

screens.title: The visit order
screens.prose: BFS processes one node at a time. It takes the earliest-found node next, and it reads each node's neighbours in alphabetical order.
screens.question: Put the nodes in the order BFS processes them, starting from A.

hints.text: A is first. Then A's neighbours, in alphabetical order.
B was found before D, so B's new neighbours come before D's.
A, then B, D. B finds E; D finds C and F. E finds G and H.

feedback.correct: A, B, D, E, C, F, G, H.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Finish each day before starting the next, in the order nodes were found.

byKey.C: You sorted day 2 by name. E was found by B, and B came before D, so E goes before C.
byKey.E: E belongs to day 2. Process B and D, all of day 1, first.
byKey.G: G is on day 3. Finish E, C and F first.

explain.text: Within a day the order is the order of discovery, not the alphabet. B came before D, so B's discovery E comes before D's C and F. A line where the first in is the first out is a **queue**.

screens.title: Inside the queue
screens.prose: A is processed: B and D were found and joined the back of the queue. Now B is processed. It leaves the front, and every neighbour not yet found joins the back.
screens.question: Drag the cards to show the queue after B is processed.

hints.text: B leaves the queue. Which of B's neighbours has not been found yet?
B's neighbours are A and E. A is already processed.
Move B to Processed. Move E to the back of the queue, after D.

feedback.correct: The queue is D, then E.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. B leaves the front, and only its new neighbour joins, at the back.

byKey.A: A is already processed. A node joins the queue once, when it is first found.
byKey.B: B has just been processed, so it leaves the queue for Processed.
byKey.E: E is B's only new neighbour. It joins at the back, behind D.
byKey.D: D was waiting before E arrived, so D stays at the front.

explain.text: A queue hands back nodes in the order they arrived. D was found before E, so D is processed next. That first-in, first-out rule is what makes BFS finish one day before the next.

screens.title: BFS step by step
screens.prose: Each node is marked **seen** the moment it joins the queue, so nothing joins twice.

steps.caption: Start: A is seen and queued.
Process A. B and D are new: mark them seen and queue them.
Process B. A is seen already; E is new.
Process D. C and F are new.
Process E. G and H are new.
C finds G already seen, so G is not queued again. The rest find nothing new.

canvas.caption: Visit order: A, B, D, E, C, F, G, H

screens.title: Write BFS
screens.prose: Return the visit order. Take neighbours in sorted order, `for v in sorted(adj[u])`, so every graph has a single right answer. Use `deque`: `popleft()` takes from the front in one step.

state.caption: `bfs(adj, "A")` should return A, B, D, E, C, F, G, H

screens.question: Write `bfs(adj, start)`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on fixed graphs. They include a start with no neighbours, a disconnected graph, a directed graph and a 3,000-node path. Neighbours must be taken in sorted order, so each answer is a single list.

hints.text: Keep three things: a `seen` set, a `deque` and the `order` list.
Mark a node seen when it is queued, as D and B were.
Pop `u` with `popleft()` and append it to `order`. For each `v` in `sorted(adj[u])` not in `seen`: add it to `seen`, then queue it.

feedback.correct: One `seen` set, one queue, and every node processed once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 is a square: D is next to both B and C. If D appears twice, mark nodes seen when you queue them, not when you pop them.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 starts at X, which has no neighbours. The answer is just `["X"]`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is a path of 3,000 nodes. A search that calls itself once per node goes 3,000 calls deep, past Python's recursion limit; use the queue loop.

explain.text: The `seen` check guards the queue, so each node is queued once. Each edge is read once from each end, so BFS is $O(V + E)$. Sorting neighbours only fixes the order for the tests.

screens.title: Marking too late
screens.prose:
This version marks a node seen when it leaves the queue, not when it joins.

```python
queue = deque(["A"])
seen, order = set(), []
while queue:
    u = queue.popleft()
    seen.add(u)
    order.append(u)
    for v in sorted(adj[u]):
        if v not in seen:
            queue.append(v)
```
screens.question: What is `order` at the end?

options.why: You expected the `seen` check to stop repeats. E queues G, and C queues G again before either copy is processed.
Each popped node is marked seen, so no node is queued after it has been processed. The queue does empty.
G and H are still reached through E. The bug adds visits; it does not lose any.

hints.text: When is G marked seen in this version?
G is a neighbour of E and of C.
E queues G. C is processed before G, sees G is not yet marked, and queues it again.

feedback.correct: G is queued twice and processed twice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the queue: G is a neighbour of both E and C.

byKey.right: You assumed `seen` blocks the second copy of G. G is only marked once popped, and C runs before that.
byKey.loop: You expected an infinite loop. Popped nodes are marked, so nothing is queued after it is processed.

explain.text: Between joining and leaving the queue, G is not marked, so C queues it a second time. On a dense graph a node can be queued once per neighbour, which is $O(E)$ copies. Mark a node when it joins the queue.

canvas.caption: G queued by E, then again by C

screens.title: Nodes BFS never meets
screens.prose: Two edges are gone. BFS from A follows edges only, so it cannot jump to a part with no path from A.
screens.question: Tap every node that `bfs(adj, "A")` leaves out.

hints.text: Which nodes can you still reach from A by walking along edges?
C and G are joined only to each other now.
From A you reach B, D, E, F and H. C and G form a separate piece.

feedback.correct: C and G form a separate piece, so BFS from A never finds them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow edges out from A and tap only what you cannot reach.

byKey.H: H is still joined to E, which is joined to B. BFS from A reaches it.
byKey.F: F is still joined to D, a neighbour of A.
byKey.A: A is the start, so it is the first node in the result.

explain.text: BFS returns only the start's **connected component**. C and G are unreachable, so they never enter the queue. To visit every node, start a new BFS from each node not yet seen.

canvas.caption: Reached: A, B, D, E, F, H

screens.title: The BFS pattern
screens.question: A colleague uses a plain list, `queue = [start]`, with `queue.pop(0)`. What changes on a graph of 100,000 nodes?

options.text: Each `pop(0)` shifts every remaining item, so the search can take $O(V^2)$ steps

options.why: A list keeps its items side by side, so removing the first one moves every other one left. A `deque` removes it in one step.
Both take from the front, so the order is the same. Only the cost differs.

feedback.correct: Same order, but up to $V$ shifts per pop.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what a list must do to remove its first item.

explain.text: With 100,000 nodes in the queue, each `pop(0)` moves up to 100,000 pointers. That is up to $10^{10}$ moves in all, against $10^5$ with `deque.popleft()`. The answer is right either way, which is why the bug survives testing on small graphs.

screens.title: Contagion from a default
screens.prose: Firm Cedar has defaulted. Risk treats every firm at most `k` trading links away as first in line for losses. The graph is undirected.
screens.question: Write `within_hops(adj, start, k)`: the sorted names of every firm at most `k` edges from `start`, not counting `start`.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests on counterparty graphs. They include k = 0, a k larger than the graph and a firm with no counterparties. Return the names sorted.

hints.text: Run BFS, but record each firm's distance when it is found.
Birch, Elm and Larch are 1 edge from Cedar.
Keep `dist = {start: 0}`. Do not expand a firm whose distance is already `k`. Return the sorted names other than `start`.

feedback.correct: BFS with distances stops cleanly at `k` hops.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects the firms 1 or 2 edges from Cedar. If Hazel appeared, you expanded a firm already at distance `k`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has `k = 0`: no firm other than Cedar is within 0 edges, so return `[]`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 is a triangle. Each neighbour should appear once, so mark firms when they are found.

explain.text: BFS finds each firm at its fewest hops, so `dist` is exact when a firm is first seen. Within two hops of Cedar are Alder, Birch, Elm, Fir, Larch, Oak. Fir links to Hazel, but Hazel is three hops out.

ideas: Breadth-first search processes nodes in the order they were found, using a queue. It finishes every node at distance $d$ before any at $d + 1$.
Mark a node seen when it joins the queue, and pop with `deque.popleft()`. Then BFS runs in $O(V + E)$.
BFS reaches only the start's connected component. The round a node is found in is its fewest edges from the start.

formula.name: BFS cost
formula.note: Each node joins once; each edge is read once from each end.

summary.trap: Marking a node seen only when it is popped lets it join the queue once per neighbour.

quiz.prose: BFS must finish every node at distance 1 before any node at distance 2.
quiz.question: Which structure gives it that order?

options.text: A queue: first in, first out
A stack: last in, first out
options.why: A stack hands back the newest node first, so the search dives deep instead. That is depth-first search, the next lesson.
A set has no order at all, so it cannot say which node comes next. BFS uses a set only for `seen`.

feedback.correct: Nodes leave in the order they were found.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which node the structure hands back next.

explain.text: Nodes found at distance 1 join the queue before any at distance 2. A queue hands them back in that same order, so one level finishes before the next starts.

quiz.prose: A star graph: one centre joined to 6 outer nodes, and no other edges. BFS starts at the centre.
quiz.question: How many nodes are in the queue just after the centre is processed?

feedback.correct: All 6 outer nodes are found at once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The centre leaves; each new neighbour joins.

byKey.centre: You kept the centre in the queue. It leaves when it is processed.
byKey.one: BFS queues every new neighbour of the centre, not just the first.

explain.text: Processing the centre removes it and queues each of its 6 unseen neighbours. So the queue holds 6 nodes, all at distance 1.

quiz.prose: A desk can convert only between quoted pairs. BFS from GBP over the quoted pairs first finds JPY in round 3.
quiz.question: What does that tell you?

options.text: The shortest chain of conversions from GBP to JPY uses 3 trades
The cheapest way to buy yen takes 3 trades
options.why: BFS counts edges, not costs. The cheapest chain needs each trade's cost as a weight: Dijkstra, in level 2.

options.text: There are exactly 3 chains from GBP to JPY
options.why: BFS finds the fewest edges to each node, not the number of routes.

feedback.correct: Round 3 means three edges, and no chain is shorter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. BFS rounds count edges from the start.

explain.text: A node first found in round $d$ is exactly $d$ edges from the start. So no chain shorter than 3 trades reaches JPY; lesson 6 builds on this.

options.why: You expected BFS to visit every key. It follows edges, and no edge reaches Z.
Z is a key with an empty list, and BFS never even looks it up.

feedback.correct: Z has no edges, so a search from X never reaches it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. BFS only meets nodes joined to the start by a path.

explain.text: BFS from X finds Y and stops. Z is a separate component, so it never joins the queue.
